source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models - Game of 24 main result
finding: ToT beat IO, CoT and CoT-SC by a wide margin on Game of 24 with GPT-4. Even breadth 1 gave a large gain.
numbers: Success: IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC (k=100) 9.0%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%. 100 problems (indices 901-1000 of 1362). IO best-of-100 33%, CoT best-of-100 49%.
limits: Task is shallow (3 steps), has a small exact state space and an easy rule check. Oracle best-of-k for CoT is not a deployable method.
agent_relevance: S6 idea tree can beat plain sampling when the task has short, checkable steps. Branching matters more than extra samples of one chain.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models - error analysis
finding: About 60% of CoT samples already failed after the first step (first three words, e.g. '4 + 9'). Early commitment is the failure mode that search fixes.
numbers: ~60% of CoT samples failed at step 1 on Game of 24 (GPT-4).
quote: around 60% of CoT samples already failed the task after generating the first step
limits: One task, one model.
agent_relevance: Supports branching at the first thought rather than only at the end. Matches our guardrail that doubt should hit early choices.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models - Creative Writing
finding: ToT gave a modest gain in GPT-4 coherence and was preferred by humans more often than CoT. Refinement helped further.
numbers: GPT-4 coherence score (1-10): IO 6.19, CoT 6.93, ToT 7.56; with refine IO 7.67, ToT 7.91. Human pairwise preference: ToT chosen over CoT more often than CoT over ToT (read from a figure, roughly 41 vs 21 of 100 pairs, 38 similar). 100 tasks.
limits: Scores come from GPT-4 as judge plus a small human check; no variance reported. ToT costs about 5x the tokens. Self-judged quality is open to judge bias.
agent_relevance: A vote over plans is cheap. Do not trust model coherence scores alone (guardrail G5).

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models - Mini Crosswords and ablations
finding: DFS with LLM pruning solved few full crosswords but raised word-level success a lot. Backtracking and pruning each mattered.
numbers: 5x5 crosswords, 20 games. Letter/word/game success: IO 38.7/14/0, CoT 40.6/15.6/1, ToT 78/60/20 (4 of 20 games). Oracle best state 82.4/67.5/35 (7 of 20). No prune 65.4/41.5/5. No backtrack 54.6/20/5. DFS limited to 100 steps.
limits: Even the best arm solved at most 7 of 20 games. The state evaluator wrongly pruned some correct words (GPT-4 did not know obscure words). Tiny test set.
agent_relevance: Backtracking is a real ingredient (word success 20% without it vs 60%). A weak pruner costs correct branches, so prune softly.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models - generation versus evaluation split (appendix B.2)
finding: With GPT-3.5, ToT still beat CoT but far below GPT-4. Mixed-model runs show the generator is the bottleneck on Game of 24.
numbers: Game of 24: GPT-3.5 IO 6%, CoT 3%, ToT 19%. GPT-4 generate + GPT-3.5 evaluate 64%; GPT-3.5 generate + GPT-4 evaluate 31%. Creative Writing GPT-3.5 coherence IO 4.47, CoT 5.16, ToT 6.62.
limits: Proposal prompt was changed from 1-shot to 3-shot for GPT-3.5 to make it work, so conditions differ.
agent_relevance: A cheap judge can score a strong generator's thoughts. Spend the strong model on proposing.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models - GSM8K and StrategyQA (appendix B.1)
finding: On easy benchmarks where CoT already works, ToT adds little.
numbers: GPT-4, 100 questions each. GSM8K: IO 51, CoT 86, ToT 90. StrategyQA: IO 73, CoT 82, ToT 83.
limits: The authors note the bottleneck of StrategyQA is knowledge, not reasoning. With n=100 a 1 to 4 point gain is within noise.
agent_relevance: Do not open an idea tree on problems a single chain already solves. Trigger search on a failed check only (G1).

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models - cost (appendix B.3)
finding: ToT costs about as much as 100 CoT samples on Game of 24 and about 5x on Creative Writing; the authors say 5-100x more generated tokens than CoT.
numbers: Game of 24: ToT 5.5k completion tokens at 74%; CoT best-of-100 6.7k tokens at 49%; IO best-of-100 1.8k at 33%. Per-case dollar figures in the PDF text are garbled but ToT is the most expensive row. Creative Writing: ToT 4k completion tokens vs CoT 0.9k.
limits: Cost table text is partly garbled in extraction; token counts above are the readable ones.
agent_relevance: Idea tree needs a hard token budget; code should cap breadth and depth.

source: Long (2023) Large Language Model Guided Tree-of-Thought
finding: Independent concurrent ToT with a rule-based checker and controller for Sudoku. A code checker detects dead ends and triggers backtracking. Gains over one-shot and few-shot.
numbers: Sudoku: ToT solved all ten 3x3; 4x4 solved 9 of 10; 5x5 solved 8 of 10. Authors say ToT beat the best of one-shot/few-shot by 11% (3x3), 80% (4x4), 60% (5x5), as stated by them. Max 100 conversation rounds.
limits: Tiny sets (10 puzzles each), preliminary paper, no cost data.
agent_relevance: Closest to our design: code checks validity and the controller decides backtracking, the model only proposes. A hard checker removes self-evaluation noise.

source: Sel et al. (2023) Algorithm of Thoughts
finding: Putting a search trace inside one prompt matched or beat ToT at a small fraction of the calls. It also reports ToT at 69%, not 74%, when it re-ran ToT.
numbers: Game of 24: IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC 9.0%, ToT b=5 69% (109.1 queries), AoT 71% (1 query). 5x5 crosswords word success: ToT 46.5% (>200 queries) vs AoT 52% (2 queries); CoT-SC 15.6%.
limits: ToT figures were re-run by the authors, not the original 74%. AoT needs hand-written algorithm examples and was tested on the same few tasks.
agent_relevance: A one-pass prompt can imitate search cheaply; useful as a low-budget fallback beside an explicit tree.

source: Besta et al. (2023/2024) Graph of Thoughts
finding: Letting thoughts merge (aggregation) beat ToT on tasks that decompose and recombine, such as sorting.
numbers: Authors report sorting quality 62% better than ToT and cost >31% lower than ToT (ChatGPT-3.5).
limits: Sorting and set operations are decomposable by design; gains depend on tasks with a merge step. Authors designed the baselines.
agent_relevance: Our S6 tree could add a merge step (combine two ideas) when subproblems are independent.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
finding: MCTS with a model-simulated world state beat chain of thought on Blocksworld; with LLaMA-33B it beat GPT-4 CoT.
numbers: Blocksworld success by plan length (2/4/6 step): CoT GPT-4 0.50/0.63/0.40; RAP(10) 1.00/0.86/0.26; RAP(20) 1.00/0.88/0.42. Average RAP 64% (LLaMA-33B).
limits: Blocksworld is small and has an exact state; RAP still costs many calls per problem. GSM8K gains were smaller.
agent_relevance: Explicit state tracking plus search helps where actions change a state. Prefer a code-held state when the task has one.

source: Xie et al. (2023) Self-Evaluation Guided Beam Search for Reasoning
finding: Step-level self-evaluation used to prune a stochastic beam gave modest gains over baseline decoding and was cost-efficient at equal tokens.
numbers: Codex few-shot: GSM8K 85.5 vs 80.4, AQuA 64.2 vs 58.6, StrategyQA 77.2 vs 73.2. At equal budget GSM8K 46.1% (12.6k tokens) vs self-consistency 41.8% (13.9k). Single-chain version costs ~3x SC with n=16 rollouts.
limits: Gains of 3-6 points on strong baselines; smaller where answers are less diverse (SVAMP +0.7).
agent_relevance: Step-level self-scores give small gains. Treat them as a tie-breaker, not as the main selector.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Reasoning in Token Economies: Budget-Aware Evaluation of LLM Reasoning Strategies
finding: The key budget-matched check. With GPT-3.5 on Game of 24, simple self-consistency beat ToT. Only with GPT-4 did ToT win, and it needed a large budget.
numbers: Game of 24, GPT-4: ToT b=5 top1 74% (best-of-all 76%), b=3 77%, b=1 65%; CoT 100 samples top1 17%, best-of-all 56%. GPT-3.5: ToT b=5 top1 25% (best 35%) vs CoT-100 top1 4% (best 46%); SC beats ToT on GPT-3.5 by a clear margin.
limits: Game of 24 plus 5 other datasets for other methods; GPT-3.5 evaluator prompt was modified. The paper says gains of fancy methods often vanish at equal budget.
agent_relevance: Compare any idea tree against plain self-consistency at equal tokens before keeping it. Tree wins only if the proposer model is strong.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Reasoning in Token Economies - evaluator ablation
finding: The ToT evaluator carries real weight but a cheap evaluator nearly matches the expensive one.
numbers: Game of 24, 100 instances, GPT-4 proposer: GPT-4 evaluator 76%, $159.87; GPT-3.5 evaluator 72%, $33.53; b=1 GPT-4 evaluator 65%, $49.9; evaluate-once drops accuracy; random evaluator best-of-all 4%. GPT-3.5 proposer + GPT-4 evaluator only 38%.
limits: Single task. A random pruner is a harsher control than no pruning.
agent_relevance: Evaluator quality matters but a code checker or small model suffices. Evaluate each thought several times, not once.

source: Katz et al. (2024) Thought of Search: Planning with Language Models Through The Lens of Efficiency
finding: Asking the LLM to write the successor function and goal test as code, then running plain BFS, solved Game of 24 at 100% with a handful of LLM calls. ToT's per-state LLM calls are mostly unnecessary.
numbers: Game of 24: all 1362 instances correct (1361 solvable, 1 correctly flagged unsolvable); 5 generated implementations ran in 1.92-6.83 s total. Crosswords: 20/20 solved (with 10 candidate answers per clue assumed). Estimated GPT-4-turbo cost: $40 for IO/CoT, $14,000 for RAP, $16,000 for LATS. ToT quoted at 75% on a 100-problem subset.
limits: Requires an exact, coded state and rules; the crossword test assumed candidate answers (author-stated). Does not cover open-ended tasks.
agent_relevance: Strongest boundary: when the state space can be coded, let the program search and the model only write the checker. Matches schema section 1.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally
finding: Tree-style search against a process reward model (beam, lookahead) helps at low budget and on hard questions but not on easy ones or at high budget.
numbers: MATH, PaLM-2 with PRM. Beam search beats best-of-N at low generation budget; at larger budgets the gain shrinks and beam falls below best-of-N. Lookahead search generally underperforms at equal budget. By difficulty: levels 1-2 beam search degrades with more budget; levels 3-4 beam beats best-of-N; level 5 no method makes progress. Compute-optimal allocation about 4x more efficient than best-of-N.
limits: Needs a trained PRM; the over-optimisation seen (short, repetitive steps) is the PRM being exploited, so findings partly depend on the verifier.
agent_relevance: Match search effort to difficulty: more search only after a check fails on a hard item. A strong learned scorer can be exploited.

source: Wu et al. (2024/2025) Inference Scaling Laws: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-Optimal Inference
finding: MCTS was a poor compute trade versus plain sampling in their setup; a simpler tree search (REBASE) was better. A smaller model plus search can beat a bigger model.
numbers: MATH500/GSM8K, Llemma-7B/34B. REBASE better than sampling and MCTS at all budgets; Llemma-7B + REBASE beats Llemma-34B with majority voting at all budgets and gets competitive accuracy with about 2x less compute. MCTS uses dozens of times more generated tokens, partly spent on node evaluation.
limits: Math tasks with a trained reward model; MCTS configuration details matter.
agent_relevance: Tree search is not automatically better than sampling. Spend tokens on candidate paths, not on estimating nodes.

source: Bi et al. (2024/2025) Forest-of-Thought: Scaling Test-Time Compute for Enhancing LLM Reasoning
finding: Several independent trees plus self-correction beat one big ToT at the same cost. Making ToT wider hit diminishing returns.
numbers: Game of 24: base ToT without add-ons 10.58% in their ablation (Llama3-8B-Instruct); full FoT 96.84% in the final table; Table 2 lists ToT b=5 at 74.00% (taken from Yao), IO 10.22%, CoT 4.38%. Widening ToT to 32 leaves gives no further gain. 4-rollout MCTSr with 2 trees was 3.2% better than 8-rollout MCTSr.
limits: The ToT row in the main table is copied from the original paper (GPT-4) while their own method uses a small model, so the comparison is mixed. Authors' own method, not independent.
agent_relevance: Diversity of trees can beat depth of one tree, and one tree saturates. Consistent with G4: samples from one model are correlated.

source: Ding et al. (2023/2024) Everything of Thoughts (XoT)
finding: An independent re-run of ToT found lower Game of 24 accuracy than the original (60.6% at b=3, 34.3% at b=1 with GPT-4) and weak results on 8-Puzzle and Pocket Cube, where an MCTS-trained policy beat ToT by a large gap.
numbers: Game of 24 (GPT-4): IO 10.22, CoT 4.38, CoT-SC 4.38, ToT b=1 34.31 (23.5 LLM calls), ToT b=3 60.58 (39.83 calls), GoT 10.95, XoT 85.40 with 3 revisions. GPT-3.5 ToT b=3 10.22. 8-Puzzle GPT-4: ToT b=3 13.45, XoT 95.80. Pocket Cube GPT-4: ToT b=3 19.57.
limits: Different test set and prompts from the original; authors promote their own method, so this is an adversarial re-run. It shows ToT does not transfer to longer-horizon puzzles.
agent_relevance: ToT numbers depend heavily on prompt and test set. Do not expect 74% to carry over to long-horizon tasks.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2023) GPT-4 Doesn't Know It's Wrong: An Analysis of Iterative Prompting for Reasoning Problems
finding: On graph colouring, GPT-4 was about as bad at verifying solutions as at finding them, and the content of the critique did not matter. This undercuts the self-evaluation step in ToT.
numbers: Graph colouring: no-feedback baseline ~16% correct; with back-prompting up to ~40%; generic re-prompting with no real critique gave about the same ~40%; GPT-4 marked only 10% of instances as non-optimal in one verification set. Gains come from the right answer appearing among top-k samples plus an external verifier.
limits: One NP-complete problem family, GPT-4 only; ToT evaluation (can this partial state reach 24) is a slightly different judgement.
agent_relevance: Where possible use a code verifier in place of an LLM value judgement. Resampling can look like critique-driven gain.

source: Huang et al. (2023/2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without external feedback, self-correction did not help and sometimes hurt reasoning. This is the same weakness a ToT self-evaluator relies on.
numbers: GSM8K: GPT-3.5 kept its first answer 74.7% of the time after two rounds of self-correction; among changes, more correct answers became wrong than the reverse. CommonSenseQA and Llama-2: frequent correct-to-incorrect flips.
limits: Intrinsic self-correction only; with oracle or code feedback the picture differs.
agent_relevance: Support for G2: revise only from real output. Judge by code, not by the model's opinion.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2024) LLMs Still Can't Plan; Can LRMs? A Preliminary Evaluation of OpenAI's o1 on PlanBench
finding: Planning benchmarks resist plain prompting. A model trained to reason inside its output (o1) did far better than earlier LLMs on PlanBench but was not saturated and not robust.
numbers: Best LLM on regular Blocksworld: LLaMA 3.1 405B 62.6%. Mystery Blocksworld (renamed predicates): no LLM above 5%. o1-preview much higher but not saturated.
limits: Preliminary one-week evaluation. Does not test ToT prompting directly; it shows the ceiling for prompt-only planning.
agent_relevance: Scaffolds may matter less as models absorb search into their own reasoning; keep the scaffold light.

source: Gandhi et al. (2024) Stream of Search (SoS): Learning to Search in Language
finding: Training a small model on full search traces (including dead ends and backtracking) beat training on only optimal solutions on Countdown, a generalisation of Game of 24. The authors expect external ToT to stay more efficient short term.
numbers: Countdown, 250M GPT-Neo, 500k problems. Held-out inputs: SoS 51.27% vs optimal-path model 25.73% (about +25 points). SoS solved 36% of previously unsolved problems. Dataset: 285,501 of 500k trajectories (57.1%) reach the goal.
limits: Needs training; one synthetic task; not a prompting study.
agent_relevance: Our agent cannot train, so keep the search outside the model as program-controlled branching.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1 (unsuccessful attempts, appendix)
finding: Authors tried MCTS over reasoning steps to scale test-time compute and gave up: search space is too large and a fine-grained value model is hard to train. Long chain of thought won.
numbers: No accuracy numbers given for the MCTS attempt. They state MCTS can improve inference performance with a pre-trained value model but iterative self-improvement through self-search remains a significant challenge.
limits: Negative result in prose without numbers; about training, not prompting.
agent_relevance: For strong reasoning models, a hand-built tree may add little; test the tree against the model's own long reasoning before keeping it.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models - search design choices
finding: The paper separates three choices: how to generate thoughts (sample i.i.d. vs propose sequentially), how to evaluate (value each state vs vote across states), and the search algorithm (BFS b=5 for 24 and writing, DFS with a 100-step cap for crosswords).
numbers: Game of 24: 3 steps, b=5, each state valued 3 times (sure/maybe/impossible). Creative writing: 5 plans sampled, 5 votes. Crosswords: DFS cap 100 steps.
limits: Design is hand-tuned per task; no study of prompt sensitivity.
agent_relevance: For S6, make branching factor, depth and number of re-evaluations explicit parameters set by code.

source: Long (2023) Large Language Model Guided Tree-of-Thought - controller limits
finding: A rule-based controller issues backtrack when the model is stuck, but it cannot tell whether a valid partial board is completable, which wastes rounds.
numbers: Sudoku 4x4: one failure of 10 within 100 rounds; 5x5: 2 failures of 10, blamed by the authors on the controller.
limits: Cause is the authors' suspicion, not tested; neural controller left to future work.
agent_relevance: Dead-end detection in code needs a completability test, not only a rule check.
